title: The poet from the anthill
hook: a poet named after an anthill, and the robber turned around by Rama's name
carry: nama japa: repeating God's name can remake a life

segments.voice: Yesterday: the whole story in chapter one, and your line: the Ramayana is read for dharma, not suspense.

Valmika is a Sanskrit word for an anthill, the tall mound of earth termites and ants build. Tradition hears the poet's name, Valmiki, as the one from the anthill. Why would anyone be named that? There's a story people tell, a story of a changed life, told across India in many languages. But here's the honest part: Valmiki's own Ramayana doesn't tell it. In his own book he is simply a hermit, living by a river, asking a good question.

segments.voice: Start with Narada. He's a devarshi, a sage of the gods, and he turns up across Hindu storytelling. He wanders between heaven and earth, carries news, asks the question that sets things moving, and in later tradition he walks with a vina, singing the name of Vishnu. Now Valmiki. Some later texts and retellings say he began life as a highway robber, often called Ratnakara, who robbed travelers to feed his family. One day he stopped a group of sages, sometimes Narada himself. They asked: will your family share the weight of your wrongdoing? He went home and asked. They said no. Shaken, he asked the sages for help, and was given the name of Rama to repeat. He couldn't even say it properly, so he said mara, mara, which run together becomes Rama, Rama. He sat so long that an anthill rose over him, and the man who came out was Valmiki, the one from the anthill. That story is found in later works, not in Valmiki's Sanskrit text, where he is simply a muni, a quiet sage. So why do Hindus keep telling it? Because it carries a big teaching: nama japa, repeating the name of God. Many Hindu traditions hold that the name itself has power, that saying it again and again, even clumsily, turns a person toward God. That's why you'll see Hindus counting a name on a mala of a hundred and eight beads, or saying Rama, Rama under their breath. And it says something else: no one is too far gone. A robber can become the first poet. Today the Valmiki community, in North India especially, honors him as its own guru.

segments.voice: Hindus often repeat a sacred name with the breath, sometimes on a mala. If you pray, choose a name sacred to you, Rama or another, and say it softly on each out-breath; if the words get jumbled, let them. The robber's did. If you don't pray, repeat one quiet word, like peace, and come back to it whenever you drift.
Valmika, an anthill. Valmiki's name means the one from the anthill, and Narada is the wandering sage of the gods who answers his question.
Your line: nama japa, repeating God's name can remake a life. Even a jumbled mara, mara became Rama, Rama. Until tomorrow.
